blogs.title: Reasoning across millions of documents
blogs.author: Kush Madlani
blogs.description: How Fact Intelligence prepares the entire case record in advance, helping lawyers find and connect facts across millions of documents.
blogs.content: A large commercial dispute runs to hundreds of thousands of documents and tens of millions of pages. At that scale, AI can fail quietly: the answer cites real sources and is still wrong, because the model never saw the document that contradicts it. Fact Intelligence takes a different approach. It reads every page in advance and turns the record into connected, source-linked facts, so the Legora Agent works from the whole case rather than a sample. Fact Intelligence makes that possible across millions of documents. Why scale breaks legal AI Three problems decide whether an AI tool is useful on a large matter. None is solved by a new model alone. They are properties of the work. A model only reasons over what it can see A million-token context window holds roughly 1,500 pages of evidence, depending on the documents. Against a disclosure set of tens of millions of pages, that is a fraction of a percent. Every model call therefore embeds a selection decision: what the model sees, and what it doesn't. If retrieval misses, the model can reason confidently from an incomplete record. Reading the record costs more than querying it Scanned PDFs, photographed documents, and faxes need optical character recognition (OCR) to become searchable text. Documents then need parsing, classification, extraction, and indexing. That preparation is where much of the compute goes. The same event appears many times An email instructs finance to release a payment on March 14. A ledger records a transfer on March 15. A witness statement says the supplier was paid "the following week." These may describe the instruction and settlement of one payment, or separate payments. Working out which is the difference between a chronology and a list of fragments. How Fact Intelligence works at scale Read the record before the Agent does When a file arrives, Fact Intelligence works out what it is before extracting the facts. A transcript is read with awareness of who is speaking. An email is reconstructed in sending order and kept with its attachments as a family. A message thread is reassembled across days. A spreadsheet is read cell by cell. Speaker attribution and cell relationships are part of the evidence. Routing every page through a frontier model is the fastest way to exhaust a matter budget before ingestion finishes. Where older techniques do the job better and cheaper, we use them: splitting documents by meaning, finding the most information-dense passages, and spotting where defined terms cluster. Models are reserved for the steps that need them. The main one is fact extraction itself, which runs on every page through a gated pipeline where each step verifies the last. The work runs in parallel across compute that scales up for a large production and shuts down when it is done. Process each document once, cite every copy The same attachment may be forwarded by five people. Identical content is processed once, but each copy still matters, because who sent it and where it sat is evidence in its own right. So a fact extracted once is cited to every document it appears in, and the folder structure the team uploaded stays exactly as it was. Reconcile facts without comparing everything to everything Comparing every fact against every other fact doesn't scale: with 100,000 facts, that means billions of comparisons. Each fact is reduced to a short signature designed so that similar facts produce similar signatures. Only facts whose signatures are close are compared. Reducing comparisons is only part of the problem. The comparison work also has to fit in memory. We divide it into bounded groups that workers process independently, rather than loading the whole record at once. Larger groups use approximate nearest-neighbor search to identify candidate matches. blogs.author: Adrian Parlow
blogs.description: Our engineering output tripled in three months once enough of the right pieces were in place. In-house legal work is heading for the same kind of step change.
blogs.content: Our engineering output tripled in three months once enough of the right pieces were in place. In-house legal work is heading for the same kind of step change. We're approaching an inflection point in how much legal work AI can complete on its own. I expect the result to be a step change in productivity: many legal tasks run autonomously and in-house teams get far more done with the people they have. For legal departments asked to support a growing business without growing headcount, that changes what the team can take on. Our introduction to this series made the case that when legal work gets cheaper and faster, more of it becomes worth doing. This post covers the product thinking behind that. I use coding as the analog throughout, because it's the one place where we see both sides: we build software ourselves, and we work with in-house legal teams every day. Our engineering team hit a tipping point this year AI for coding has consistently run six to twelve months ahead of legal, and in March we wrote that legal was tracking the same curve as software development, one cycle behind. Our own engineering team offers a glimpse of where legal is heading. For most of the past year, the amount each engineer shipped was improving at a slow and steady pace, even as the underlying models kept getting better. Then all of a sudden, between July and October the number of code changes we shipped to production more than tripled. In less than three months, we saw a dramatic increase in velocity that could not be attributed to increased headcount. These productivity improvements tend to come gradually and then all of a sudden. Once enough of the right ingredients are in place a tipping point is reached and progress increases exponentially. For us, the final ingredient was our cloud agent setup. Once an agent running in the cloud could take a change all the way to production, our engineers could massively parallelize their work, running many agents at once instead of working on just one or a few things at a time. Legal work is approaching the same tipping point I believe legal work is about to see the same kind of step change as software engineering. Right now we're in the gradual improvement stage, improving each of the individual ingredients. I expect it to keep looking like slow progress right up until it changes rapidly. Three things had to be good enough before our engineering team reached its tipping point, and the same three have to be good enough in legal. Ingredient What tipped engineering What it takes in legal Models Good enough to write the code Good enough to do the legal reasoning Tools Cloud agents that take a change all the way to production Building blocks that complete a workflow end to end Setup A clean, modular codebase with tests and automated checks Your processes, playbooks and policies codified into the system The models are improving every month as the labs race toward superintelligence. Building the tools that enable end-to-end legal work is our job at Legora. The third is up to each legal department: getting its own setup ready for agents, with help from the tools it uses. Legal work is made of a small set of building blocks Let's start with the tools. Like most knowledge work, legal is composed of a discrete set of jobs to be done. Take a given legal task and break it down into the components needed to complete it. Do that across everything a legal department handles and you don't end up with hundreds of building blocks; you end up with maybe a few dozen, falling into roughly four categories: The agent. Intelligence on tap. Agents are comprised of the model and the harness around it: the software that lets it plan, use tools and check its work. Data and context. blogs.content: Al Tamimi & Company has made Legora part of its working practice, from legal research and drafting to translation between English and Arabic. Chairman and Founder Essam Al Tamimi says the partnership reflects the UAE’s ambition to become a leader in AI, and its investment to get there. He says the firm wants to be part of that drive, and that Legora will fill “a very important part” of it.“It’s not translation, it’s not a search engine,” he says. “It goes beyond that.” That matters most in legal Arabic; Vincent Percival, Senior Knowledge Translation, explains that the work is not just about converting terms from one language to another. “You’re translating one legal system to another legal system,” he says. Getting that right is the test, and the team has seen Legora pass it. Mariam Sabet, Partner, Corporate Commercial, found that when she checked an Arabic text against Legora’s own translation, “it got it right.” Speed is the other benefit. Mohammad Al Muhtaseb, Partner, Dispute Resolution, describes a recent matter in which the team had to file around 500 pages across several reports and memoranda within three days. Legora gave the team the comfort that they would meet the deadline, and the result surprised even them. “We were amazed that we were able to do it,” he says. Malak Nasredinne, Senior Associate, explains how lawyers who once expected to spend a whole night on a task can now run it through Legora for a first draft. Essam sees the same shift in research. He says lawyers can now leave his office at midday and be back by two or three with a summary of the research. Mariam adds that some of the associates she works with have become “much more analytical” and are looking at issues in greater depth, because Legora “actually really challenges you.” For Al Tamimi, Legora is part of how the firm intends to lead in a region that is investing seriously in AI. “We believe in Legora’s system,” Essam says, and he looks forward to a continued relationship.

blogs.content: Every fact in your case, traced to its source. Litigation turns on facts. Yet establishing them means piecing together evidence scattered across thousands of emails, contracts, transcripts, and witness statements. Accounts conflict, dates are disputed, and a single detail buried in the record can change the case. Today, we're introducing Fact Intelligence , a new way for litigation teams to turn complex case records into connected, source-linked facts. Lawyers can establish what happened, investigate conflicting accounts, and test their position against the evidence. From documents to facts General-purpose AI models struggle with the scale and complexity of litigation evidence. A case record can contain far more information than a model can process at once, so AI typically relies on search and retrieval to select the material relevant to each question. But when facts are scattered across documents, important connections can be missed. Fact Intelligence takes a different approach. When case documents are uploaded, it processes the evidence before the first question is asked. It extracts reported facts, identifies the people and dates involved, and connects related information across documents, preserving links to the original sources. This creates a structured factual record that the Legora Agent can investigate. Rather than reconstructing the context from scratch with every question, the Agent can work from connected facts across the evidence, helping lawyers explore relationships, investigate inconsistencies, and verify findings against the source material. Investigate the facts, build the case With the facts connected across the record, lawyers can investigate questions that would otherwise require extensive manual review. Build chronologies of what happened and when. Bring events together across documents, with each entry linked to its source. Trace how events unfolded, identify disputed dates, and establish a clearer sequence of events. Establish who knew what, and when . Follow people, events, and communications across the record to understand when information was shared, who was involved, and how accounts developed over time. Uncover conflicting accounts. Surface inconsistencies between witness statements, emails, and other evidence. Examine competing versions of events side by side, with the original sources available to verify each finding. Test your position against the evidence. Investigate the facts that support an argument and those that could undermine it. Examine whether a witness statement or draft pleading holds against the record, and identify the points that need closer scrutiny. Instead of manually piecing together the story, lawyers can spend more time interpreting the evidence, assessing its implications, and deciding how to build the strongest case. From facts to argument Understanding the facts is only the beginning. The real value comes from putting them to work. By bringing Fact Intelligence together with Legal Research, lawyers can assess how the law applies to the specific facts of their case. That same factual understanding can inform statements of facts, briefs, witness preparation, and case strategy, with the evidence behind each finding available for review. We're building toward a more connected litigation experience in Legora, where lawyers can move from investigating the evidence to applying the law and developing their arguments in one place. blogs.title: Legal was the top AI user in the company. I couldn't prove it was working.
blogs.author: Mark Allen
blogs.description: Legora is the collaborative AI powering lawyers to review and research faster, draft smarter, and advise with precision. Legora adapts to your ways of working, unlocking team and machine collaboration at scale.
blogs.content: At one of my last in-house roles, a meeting appeared on my calendar out of the blue. Our VP of AI engineering led it, and the question was simple: the CEO wanted to know how every org in the company was benefiting from AI. Using it was no longer enough. He wanted impact, team by team, and he wanted it quarterly. Engineering wanted it monthly. Nobody had to tell them legal was using it. They had pulled usage data by department across the whole company, and legal came out on top. Then they asked what it had actually done for us, and I did not have a good answer. “It helps us mitigate risk for the company,” I said. “What does that mean?” they asked. Not having a great answer at the time felt like a personal failure. It turns out to be closer to the industry's default setting. Axiom found that 83% of in-house teams cannot measure whether their AI spending is working, and that only 7% have moved past piloting into actually using, optimizing and measuring what they bought. The framework nobody asked me to build I had seen the question coming a year earlier. When we made the case to give the whole legal department licenses to a general-purpose frontier AI assistant (the one you are probably thinking of), my GC never asked me to justify it. I built the justification anyway, because I wanted something on paper if the question ever came back around. Three categories: risk mitigation, cost savings, time savings. Every person who wanted access submitted their use cases against it. But the question was back. And the framework did not save me. The answer I gave in that room, it helps us mitigate risk, was category one of my own framework read straight back to them. The categories were right. What I never built underneath them were the baseline metrics. We had not measured where the work stood before the rollout, and we had never agreed with finance on how a risk rating converts into a dollar figure. So I could name what we were doing and I could not measure it. Part of the problem was how the original business case got built. People estimated their own savings, because there was nothing else to estimate from. Tool consolidation was part of the case too. Someone would look at a the compliance and audit platform we paid six figures a year for, expect that AI could handle most of what it did, and conclude we could probably drop it. Sometimes that turned out to be true, and we did retire a few vendors. But "probably" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and a year later, in front of engineering and finance, that business case does not hold. This was not our first attempt, either. An earlier AI pilot went out to about thirty people with an instruction I will never give again: apply this to your day-to-day work and tell us whether it delivers impactful efficiency gains. Impactful efficiency gains is not a measurable thing. People came back and said it worked here, it missed there, the output was thinner than they expected. Out of those thirty people, only a few had use cases that were genuinely ripe. We did not move forward. Adoption stops counting Here is what took me too long to accept. High adoption was not evidence that the strategy was working. It was evidence that people liked the tool. Adoption is the right metric while you are experimenting. You want to know whether anyone will touch the thing. It stops being sufficient the moment the spend gets big enough for someone outside your department to notice, and AI spend is getting there fast. Nine in ten people logging in tells a CFO nothing, in the same way that telling an engineer a risk dropped from a level five to a level four tells them nothing. The gap shows up across the market. blogs.content: Legatics , the transaction management platform used by leading law firms around the world, today announced that it has joined Legora’s product integration ecosystem . The integration connects Legatics to Legora , so lawyers working in Legora can see the current state of their deals in Legatics and make changes to them without switching between the two. Legora is the agentic operating system for legal work. Many of those lawyers are using it for review and drafting on the same complex transactions they are running in Legatics. The information about those transactions, such as what is outstanding, who is responsible for it, what has been signed and what has changed, sits in Legatics. Connecting the two means the Legora Agent can work from that information directly and put the results of its work back onto the deal, where the rest of the deal team, the client and the other side can see it and act on it. What the integration does Ask questions of the live deal. Legora can read matter data held in Legatics, including the status of checklists and trackers, who is responsible for each item, parties, deadlines, comments left by the deal team, and the contents of data rooms and closing binders. A lawyer can ask where a single deal stands or which of their matters need attention this week, and the answer comes from Legatics as it is at that moment. This makes routine reporting much quicker. An associate asked by a partner or client for a status update can have Legora pull the open items, owners and latest comments from Legatics and draft the update in minutes. Update live deals in Legatics, directly from Legora. Legora can also create and update content in Legatics. For example, a lawyer can do the following directly on Legora: review a facility agreement in Legora and create a conditions precedent checklist in Legatics from the Conditions Precedent schedule update the status of checklist items in Legatics as documents are reviewed in Legora record follow-ups from a document review in Legora on a Legatics list, with owners and deadlines build a closing checklist, issues list or documents list in a Legatics matter, with the right columns and starter rows Once that content is in Legatics, it is tracked like everything else on the deal, so the next time someone asks where things stand, the answer is updated to reflect work done in Legora. Legora can only see or change what the individual user can already see or change in Legatics. Write access is optional and is switched on by the firm. Every change made through the integration is recorded in the matter’s audit trail, and administrators can turn the connection off at any time. The integration is available to all mutual customers at no additional cost. “Lawyers want their AI tools to work from the deal as it actually stands, and then do something useful with what they find. Being able to read from Legatics is helpful, but being able to write back to it is what moves a transaction forward. Legora Agent can now do both, under the same permissions firms already rely on for everyone working on the matter,” said Anthony Seale, Founder and CEO of Legatics. “This came directly from our mutual customers. Their lawyers are doing more and more of their analysis and drafting in Legora, but the deal itself is run in Legatics, and copying work from one to the other by hand costs time and means things get missed. We think of Legatics as the infrastructure transactions run on, whether the work is done by a person or an agent, and connecting it to Legora with read and write from the start is an important part of that,” said Rob MacAdam, Chief Product & Strategy Officer at Legatics. “AI is most useful on a transaction when it knows where the deal really stands. blogs.title: How Skills and subagents work together in Legora
blogs.author: Tom Davies
blogs.description: Skills bring your team
blogs.content: Legal work draws on several kinds of expertise at once. When reviewing an agreement, a lawyer applies legal knowledge alongside the team’s review method, the client’s negotiating positions, and drafting conventions. Those inputs inform one another, and all need to be considered in the wider context of the work being done. Skills help the Legora Agent work in a similar way. They allow legal teams to capture and deploy their standards and processes as reusable instructions and supporting materials for the Agent. Skills are modular: the Agent can call on a research methodology, report drafting guidelines, and a client communication style as needed, combining them to carry out an assignment. Some parts of legal work benefit from separate execution. Legora uses subagents where that separation helps, including parallel investigations in legal research . Skills equip the Agent with reusable expertise; subagents allow it to delegate parts of an assignment. Adding expertise and dividing work are different design decisions. Applying team standards with Skills A team might create a Skill for its agreement-review process, another for client-specific guidance, and a third for drafting conventions. Each can be maintained separately and reused across assignments. The Agent applies those Skills together during a review. The review instructions guide what to examine, the client’s negotiating positions inform the recommendation, and the drafting conventions shape how it is expressed. This modularity allows the same drafting Skill to support an agreement review, a research report, or a client update. Teams can refine each body of guidance independently and combine it with others as the assignment requires. Applying another area of expertise does not, by itself, require a separate worker. Using subagents where they improve the outcome Some assignments benefit from dividing work. A legal research question spanning several jurisdictions, for example, can be broken into separate investigations that proceed in parallel. Legora uses subagents for this kind of research. Each receives a task and relevant context, then returns focused findings for the Agent to bring into the wider analysis. A separate working context can also keep extensive intermediate research from overwhelming the main analysis. Choosing when to delegate Asking a colleague to investigate a separate jurisdiction can be a sensible division of work. Asking another colleague to take over a review solely to apply a writing style introduces a handoff for something the reviewing lawyer could apply directly. In either case, delegation requires a brief and a way to incorporate the returned work. The same considerations apply to agents. Each subagent needs enough context to carry out its task, and its findings must be incorporated into the wider analysis. These steps can require additional model calls and tokens. If relevant information is omitted from the brief or the findings returned, the quality of the completed work can also suffer. Legora evaluates whether the benefits of separate execution justify the coordination it requires. We assess the complete assignment: the quality of the answer, how long it takes, the resources it uses, and how much review and correction it requires. Skills and subagents give us complementary ways to improve that result. Expertise can be specialized and reused without requiring a separate worker for every specialty. Where independent execution adds value, the Agent can delegate. Our approach is to apply expertise within the ongoing work and introduce a separate worker when doing so improves the outcome. Related reading: Why Skills make the best lawyers more valuable . Book a demo to see how Skills and subagents support your team’s work in Legora.

blogs.title: Legal work, without limits
blogs.description: In-house legal teams have the ambition to shape more decisions and take on bigger challenges. AI is creating new possibilities to act on that ambition, with greater capacity and tools that adapt to how teams work. Legal work, without limits explores that opportunity and the changes needed to turn it into everyday practice.
blogs.content: Every in-house team has work it would take on with more capacity. A policy that needs updating. Agreements that deserve a closer look. A product initiative that would benefit from legal advice before a line of code is written. Instead, teams have had to make trade-offs. For years, the time needed to complete a task, or cost of engaging with outside counsel have constrained what legal teams can achieve. Then there are the systems and software lawyers use to do the work. Legal intake is tracked in a spreadsheet, contracts live in another tool, spend in a third. Each tool imposes its own limitations on how the work should be executed and managed. AI is beginning to change that equation. As more work becomes feasible, legal teams have an opportunity to rethink how the work is done, where they can deliver even more business value and how they should organize themselves to deliver it. At Legora, we call that ambition legal work, without limits : helping legal teams take on work that was previously out of reach, and shape it around how the team actually works instead of the limits of each tool. When more legal work becomes possible Much of the discussion about legal AI starts with time savings. Those gains matter but their broader significance is what they make worth doing. If reviewing an agreement takes less time, a team can examine a larger share of its contracts. If approved policy guidance becomes easier to access, colleagues can get help at the point of making a decision. If monitoring regulations requires less manual work, a periodic exercise could become a more regular part of how the business manages change. Our view is that legal will experience a version of Jevons’ Paradox: as the cost of doing work falls, demand for it grows. Lower costs, shorter waits and easier access will encourage businesses to seek more legal support. AI adoption across other functions will also accelerate business activity. As the business moves faster, legal teams have an opportunity to bring their expertise to more business-critical decisions as strategic partners. Capturing that opportunity depends on whether in-house teams can move to AI-native ways of working. Learnings from software engineering Software engineering gives us an early indication of where legal work is heading. At Legora, coding agents increasingly complete substantial pieces of work, and we are seeing huge productivity gains per engineer. Internal data shows that between July and October 2026, our engineers have more than tripled the number of code changes shipped to production. We expect legal to follow a similar trajectory as the capabilities needed for legal work mature. Our recent in-house ROI report points the same way, with 80% of participants reporting that they are accomplishing more in the same amount of time when using Legora, with 77% reallocating that saved time to higher-value legal analysis, strategy and complex judgment calls. However, faster output will expose new bottlenecks. Writing code has accelerated faster than human review and the bottleneck modern engineering teams face is in the review process. Legal teams will encounter a similar challenge. If AI produces more drafts, analyses and answers, but each requires the same amount of lawyer attention, work will get stuck in the review queue. The answer is not more reviewers. It is deciding which work needs which kind of review, building confidence and trust in the work that should not need a lawyer in the loop, and creating systems that let lawyers apply their expertise and judgment where required. That makes the next stage of adoption an organizational question, as well as a technological one. A shift to an AI-native operating model We observe three types of operating models within in-house legal today. Manual: Every task requires human initiation, execution, and review. They make it easier to start work, find relevant context, and use Legora's legal capabilities in familiar tools. Turn ad-hoc requests from Teams and Outlook into tracked work Legal requests arrive from across the business, often through Teams messages and shared inboxes. Gathering information, routing requests, and coordinating work takes valuable time away from the legal questions themselves. With Legora Intake for Teams and Outlook, colleagues can submit a request to the legal team from the tools they already use. Mention “@Legora” in Teams or email a connected shared mailbox, and Legora gathers the necessary information and turns the request into a tracked task. The Agent can then begin the work using your team's Skills and playbooks, with a lawyer accountable throughout. For Outlook requests, follow-up questions stay in the same email thread, so colleagues can respond without changing how they work. Your business gets a simple way to access legal support, while your legal team can spend less time managing requests and more time delivering advice. Find the emails and calendar context behind a matter with the Legora Agent A contract rarely contains the full negotiating history. Key instructions and concessions may sit in emails or meeting details, leaving lawyers to gather them before they can assess the latest draft. With the new Outlook email and Calendar integration, the Legora Agent can search connected emails and attachments, and find relevant calendar details. Ask it to retrieve the correspondence behind a negotiating position or identify meetings linked to a matter. The Agent can use that context alongside documents in Legora to review provisions, identify issues, and prepare drafts. It can also help draft follow-up emails or schedule meetings, with your approval before anything is sent or booked. Lawyers spend less time reconstructing a matter and more time acting on legal questions with all the supporting information right in front of them. Build, organize and analyze spreadsheets with the Legora Agent Transaction schedules, due diligence trackers, and financial data often require hours of manual preparation before lawyers can focus on the findings. With the new Legora Excel add-in , you can ask the Agent to populate templates, build formulas, format data, and create pivot tables directly in your workbook. blogs.content: Insights A Force Majeure Clause Can Excuse Your Supplier and Still Leave You Owing Your Customers by Harvey Team • Nov 25, 2026 A force majeure clause is a contract term that excuses or suspends a party's performance when an extraordinary event outside its control, such as a hurricane, war, or government order, prevents it from performing. The clause usually requires notice and may allow termination if the event lasts. Courts read these clauses by their exact words, so two contracts can answer the same storm differently. Your supplier's plant floods, and its contract excuses the delay. Your contract with your customer doesn't. Consider the example where a food distributor buys packaged ingredients from a Gulf Coast processor and commits to deliver them to a regional grocery chain. A storm may interrupt the supplier’s duty without changing the distributor’s promise. Harvey can bring the supplier and customer terms together with source citations, allowing counsel to identify exposed deliveries before deciding on notice, alternative supply, or negotiated relief. The Same Hurricane Can Trigger Different Contract Terms Hurricanes are a known seasonal risk on the Gulf Coast. That doesn't settle whether a particular shutdown qualifies for relief. The answer depends on the clause, what the event prevents, the required notice, any duty to mitigate, and the law governing the contract. In New York, for example, the Court of Appeals explained in Kel Kim Corp. v. Central Markets that general force majeure language is normally read in light of the events specifically listed. That decision involved an insurance obligation, not a hurricane. Its value here is the method: read the contract's words and the event together, rather than assuming that any serious disruption qualifies. Three illustrative supplier contracts show why a single event can produce different questions for counsel. Illustrative clause What it says What counsel must check Named-storm clause Hurricanes are listed; written written notice is due within five business days; performance may be suspended while the plant is shut Did the storm cause the delay, and was notice delivered in the specified form and time? Act-of-God clause Natural events are covered, but relief applies only when performance is prevented Was delivery prevented, or could the supplier perform another way? No force majeure clause No express contractual event-based excuse Does governing law provide a separate excuse, and who assumed the supply risk? The named-storm clause in the first row might read: "Neither party is liable for delay caused by hurricane, flood, fire, war, or government order beyond its reasonable control, provided it gives written notice within five business days and uses reasonable efforts to resume performance. Either party may terminate if the interruption lasts more than 60 days." Naming hurricanes does not eliminate questions about causation, notice, mitigation, or substitute performance. A broader clause may cover a storm, but its exact trigger still matters. The practical first read is narrow. Identify the event, the contractual threshold, the notice trigger, and the remedy. A contract obligation management process can track notice duties over time. Here the immediate decision concerns the affected product line. The Supplier's Excuse Does Not Decide the Distributor's Duties The processor’s contract permits a qualifying storm delay. The distributor’s grocery-chain agreement requires delivery by a fixed date without matching storm relief. Forwarding the processor’s notice does not suspend the distributor’s own promise. Legal compares the processor’s obligations with the distributor’s customer commitments. It checks substitute supply, risk allocation, and the distributor’s own notice duties before advising procurement. For a sale of goods governed by an applicable enactment of UCC 2-615 , commercial impracticability may excuse a seller's delayed or failed delivery in defined circumstances.

In this work, we set out to understand how the latest models perform on agentic knowledge work and how much post-training improves that performance. With Baseten, we post-trained four recently released US open-weight models – Muse Spark Open , Nemotron 3.5 Super VL , Beam 1.0 , and Inkling 2 Small – using a recipe adapted from our Harvey Tenet work. For comparison, we also post-trained GLM-5.3 , a non-US open-weight model of similar size. We evaluated each model on agent benchmarks spanning law, consulting, banking, business automation, and software engineering. Our results show that post-training leads to substantial gains in both agentic legal reasoning and task completion across the models we studied. Specifically, we find: Muse Spark Open achieves 30.3% all-pass on LAB after post-training, the highest all-pass rate reported on the benchmark thus far and the first model to surpass 30% overall . blogs.content: 12 of our candidates’ most frequently asked questions, answered by Sebastian Peters, Head of Legal Engineering, EMEA If you’re a lawyer curious about Legal Engineering, you probably have questions, and we hear the same ones in many of our conversations with candidates: How technical do I need to be? Will I still be a lawyer? How much freedom will I really have? So we asked Sebastian Peters (Head of Legal Engineering, EMEA) to answer them head on. 1. What does a Legal Engineer at Legora actually do? “I like to use a football analogy: we’re the midfielder. We run into offense with our sales team and into defense with our customer success team. We’re part of the commercial function, and have a big role to play in delivering value to our clients. We meet customers at the pilot stage, when they want to test the tool. Our job is to show them what it can do and teach them to use it themselves: demonstrating, onboarding, coaching. We stay through rollout and adoption, so everyone gets a white-glove experience from day one. Then we hand over to customer success for the long-term relationship and start again with new accounts. You’ll have a portfolio of accounts and about 80% of your time is customer-facing: onsite, on calls, running demos and workshops.” 2. How close am I to the product team? “We’re a very good approximation of our customers, so our input is highly valued by the product team. But this isn’t a product role. On a classic RACI model, we’re consulted and informed, not accountable or responsible. Think of it as 80% customer-facing and 20% that’s yours to shape. Some people use it to work closely with product and engineering. Others go into marketing and leadership: conferences, keynotes, blog posts, shaping Legora’s public narrative. Some build enablement and AI automation; others move into people management. So it’s a bit of a choose-your-own-adventure, depending on your appetite and temperament. But it all rests on the same foundation: customer work.” 3. How technical do I need to be? “You don’t need to code at all. You do need a flair for technology, real curiosity and a good grasp of how AI works. You should be able to explain, at a high level, what model architecture looks like, what context is and why it’s difficult. Technical flair, yes. Formal technical skills, no. And a related point, because the name confuses people: we’re not software engineers. We engineer the Legora platform, configuring it to solve our customers’ workflows and use cases. And we engineer the process of law itself. You can map a legal team’s process into Legora, but you can also reimagine it in an AI-native way. That’s what we mean by engineering.” 4. How do you turn legal expertise into client impact? “I usually say it’s a merge between being a lawyer and a management consultant. At level one, you show what the tool can do. At level two, you map your customer’s processes and workflows into the platform. Ultimately, Legora shouldn’t be just a vendor. We should be partners.” 5. How much commercial responsibility comes with the role? “We’re not responsible for contracts and we don’t do hard selling; our GTM team does that. Or spotting a skeptical senior stakeholder and inviting them to lunch to build the relationship. None of it is required, but it’s appreciated.” 6. blogs.content: Product Introducing Two-Way Sync With iManage Two-way sync with iManage lets lawyers save redlines, new versions, and first and final drafts directly to iManage from Harvey. by Harvey Team • Nov 20, 2026 Watch Video On a live matter, the documents never stop moving. A counterparty markup comes back, a term gets renegotiated, a new ancillary agreement is needed. Each change runs through several documents, and every one of them has to end up as the current version in iManage. Lawyers can already search and bring documents from iManage into Harvey to draft, compare, analyze, and then manually export back into iManage. Now they can save redlines, new versions, and first and final drafts directly to iManage from Harvey. Harvey’s two-way sync with iManage , now available in early access, lets collaborators work across a matter’s documents within Harvey. As Harvey works, output is synced back to iManage with version history intact. Users can save several documents in a single approval, and the synced Vault and iManage are updated together. The work for the matter happens in Harvey, while iManage remains the system of record. One Request. Every Change Saved in iManage Consider a deal team working from a synced Vault. When the terms are renegotiated, the lawyer asks Harvey to update the purchase agreement and schedules and review a new escrow agreement if needed. Harvey pulls the latest versions from iManage and shows what it will save: two new versions and one new document. When the lawyer approves the save, Harvey files each document back to iManage as its next version, and the Vault and iManage update together. All three documents are saved within a single approval, while earlier versions remain in each document’s history, providing a complete view of iManage version history within Harvey. The same pattern applies across a matter: responding to a counterparty markup, refreshing a diligence memo as the data room grows, or updating a litigation chronology with new transcripts. In every case, the lawyer controls when changes are saved back to iManage. Why Two-Way Sync Matters Revision is only one part of the job. Lawyers must also draw on the firm’s collective experience, review their work, and share it with colleagues. Connecting these steps creates a continuous process that strengthens both individual lawyers and the broader team. With two-way sync, you can now: Start with the firm’s knowledge. Prior agreements and comparable deals help lawyers assess language in the context of work the firm has already done. Bringing those documents from iManage into Harvey gives the lawyer relevant material to reference when drafting and reviewing a revision. Work at the scale of the matter. Legal work rarely changes only one document. Harvey carries a change through every document it touches and saves each one back as the next version, with no download and re-upload step. Keep the team working from the matter’s record. The updated agreement belongs with the documents and version history the deal team already relies on. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. As Harvey takes on more of that work, from reviewing tens of thousands of documents in a single table to working through an entire data room for a diligence memo, verification becomes the bottleneck. In most fields, the output tells you most of what you need to know. An engineer can run AI-written code. A designer can judge a screen on sight. But a diligence memo can read cleanly and still be wrong because the agent never opened a side letter or missed an amendment. The only way to know is to see how the answer was produced: what was read, what was skipped, and what it relied on. In legal, the work itself is part of the output. Today that check is the lawyer: a partner reading a draft line by line, or an associate clicking through every citation. That doesn’t scale at the speed agents now work. So we think about solving verification for legal AI across three dimensions: What Harvey checks on its own: citations, quotes, and pin cites. How Harvey shows its work, so lawyers can judge what a machine can’t: what it read, what it might have missed, and the calls it made. Where Harvey stores the record of lawyers’ reviews: who checked what, who signed off, and the sources that follow the document to the next stage. The first two localize and sharpen the lawyer’s review; the third records it. Harvey Checks What Can be Checked Some questions in legal work have a clear answer. Does this case exist? Does it say what the brief claims at that page? Is the quote accurate? A machine can answer those, so Harvey should answer them before a lawyer reads a word. In legal research, agentic search ties each answer to specific documents. Harvey Graph catches authority that has been overruled or limited. And our open-source Legal Agent Benchmark grades long-horizon legal work. Those checks work on the answers Harvey writes. The harder case is the full document a lawyer is about to sign: a 40-page brief with dozens of citations from Harvey and elsewhere. blogs.content: Technical How We Built Agentic Retrieval for Patent Research In Harvey, an agent navigates fragmented patent sources, decides what information to seek next, and conducts focused research within a bounded budget. by Zhonglei Wang and Blake Chizen • Nov 19, 2026 Patent research often requires more than finding a document. A question about a claim may depend on its history: how it changed during examination, how the applicant addressed prior art, and whether later proceedings affected its status. This is the central challenge of patent research: the answer often depends on following a record over time and deciding what to inspect next . Patent attorneys do this naturally. They start with one document, notice a later event or missing fact, open another record, and continue until the question is supported, or until they can clearly identify the remaining gap. Consider a question that sounds simple: What does claim 8 cover? A conventional retrieval system can find the patent and return claim 8 as issued. But depending on what the attorney needs to know, the question may involve: What did the application originally claim? What language appeared in the issued patent? How did the applicant distinguish the claim from prior art? Is the claim still in force today? Traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) searches a fixed index, selects relevant passages, and generates an answer. That works when the information is already in one collection and the research path is predictable. In patent research, a result may reveal another record to inspect or another fact to verify. Harvey’s patent research agent starts with a research question, identifies the information needed to answer it, and selects sources based on what they contain. As it reviews the record, each result guides the next search. The rest of this post explains why a single patent index may fall short, how Harvey’s agent selects sources, and how it uses each result to decide what to search next. Why a Single Patent Index Falls Short Patent information is scattered across sources built for different purposes. Published patents contain claims, specifications, abstracts, and drawings. Patent-office systems contain application metadata, prosecution events, Office Actions, assignments, reexaminations, and PTAB proceedings. Patent indexes support broad full-text and semantic discovery. Web sources help cover international patents, procedural materials and jurisdictional gaps. Each source also has its own boundaries and limitations. Combining these sources into one corpus would be costly to build and maintain. Each new jurisdiction or provider would require more ingestion and normalization, while a larger index alone would not tell the system what information a question needs. The system also needs to recognize when a source is incomplete, choose an alternative, and decide whether the information answers the question or calls for another search. Our Solution: Agentic Retrieval Across Patent Sources Each research task starts with the question to be answered. Harvey passes it to the patent research agent as a research objective . blogs.content: Insights Building an In-House Legal Triage Process That Resolves Routine Requests Before They Reach a Lawyer by Harvey Team • Nov 19, 2026 Legal triage is the process of assessing an incoming request for its legal risk, urgency, complexity, and required next action. For in-house teams , the decision is whether approved guidance can resolve the issue, whether a lawyer needs to review prepared work, or whether it belongs in a larger matter. Consider two requests arriving on the same afternoon: HR asks for an answer already covered by an approved policy. Procurement sends a supplier data processing agreement (DPA) with an unfamiliar provision and asks for sign-off by tomorrow. Both might be marked urgent, but they shouldn’t follow the same path. One can be resolved through existing guidance, while the other needs review of the specific facts and contract language. An effective triage process makes those distinctions consistently. The work starts with rules the legal team owns, not the form employees fill out or the software they use to send a request. 1. Decide Which Legal Requests Need a Lawyer (and Which Can be Resolved) Start by defining the possible outcomes. A request labeled “contract” tells you what the business sent, but not what your legal department needs to do. A routine NDA using approved terms is different from a supplier agreement that changes the company’s liability exposure. A useful triage system should consider both the request type and the decision required. Classify Requests by Risk, Urgency, Complexity, and Required Action A practical triage matrix has three paths. Legal should agree on the signals and owners for each before automating the process: Resolve under approved guidance: For example, an HR employee asks a routine question answered by a current, approved policy. Signals: The facts fit the policy, no exception is present, and Legal has authorized a self-service response. Action: Deliver the approved answer, record the resolution, and give the employee a route to seek clarification. Prepare for lawyer review: For example, Procurement submits a supplier DPA with a change to an approved term. Signals: The request needs legal judgment, but a playbook can identify the departure and assemble relevant context. Action: Prepare a first-pass analysis, identify the issues, and route the work to the designated reviewer. Escalate to a specialist or managed matter: For example, a cross-border hiring question raises employment and privacy issues, or a product launch involves several legal workstreams. Signals: Multiple jurisdictions, new legal questions, significant exposure, or cross-functional approvals. Action: Assign the right counsel and track the related tasks and decisions. The categories should reflect the business and its risk tolerance. Urgency matters, but it isn’t a substitute for assessing legal exposure. A low-risk question due this afternoon might make sense for self-service, while a less time-sensitive request could require counsel because the underlying issue is novel or consequential. Set Escalation Rules Before Automating Triage For each category, document what the process is allowed to do, which sources it can rely on, and the point where a person needs to take over. A useful escalation rubric can flag: A requested position that falls outside an approved policy, clause, or fallback. Missing or contradictory facts that prevent a defensible decision. Sensitive data, an unfamiliar jurisdiction, or a potentially material financial or regulatory impact. A question that calls for new legal interpretation, an exception approval, or a business commitment that Legal hasn't delegated. We recommend assigning an owner and backup for every escalation path. Legal should also be able to override an automated classification and update the underlying rule. An unanswered or ambiguous request isn’t a failure of triage. blogs.content: Insights What to Check in a Data Processing Agreement Before Procurement Signs Off by Harvey Team • Nov 18, 2026 A data processing agreement (DPA) sets the contractual rules for how a vendor processes personal data on another organization’s behalf. Procurement may have agreed on the price and service levels, but the DPA still needs a separate check. What data will the supplier handle? Can it use that data for anything else? What happens if a breach or compliance request comes in? However, a DPA can contain every expected heading and still leave the organization exposed. Before signature, your legal department needs to confirm that the document reflects the actual processing arrangement, includes the protections required by applicable law, and sends any material deviation from approved standards to the person authorized to decide it. Here’s what to check before procurement moves forward. When is a Data Processing Agreement Required? Under Article 28 of the GDPR , a controller engaging a processor to handle personal data on its behalf needs to put a binding processing contract or other legal act in place. The controller determines why and how personal data will be processed and the processor acts on the controller’s instructions. The Irish Data Protection Commission’s guidance makes it clear that the agreement must identify the processing and include specific contractual duties, not just a general promise to comply with privacy law. The need for a particular agreement depends on the parties’ actual roles and the laws or jurisdictions that apply. For example, a vendor might be a processor for the service it provides and an independent controller for a separate activity. U.S. rules can also require specific vendor terms, such as California’s CCPA regulations , which prescribe contractual restrictions and specified business purposes for service providers and contractors. Those provisions aren't the same as GDPR Article 28 mentioned above. Additionally, a nondisclosure agreement protects confidential information but does not replace a required DPA. Likewise, standard contractual clauses used for international data transfers address a different legal question and may be required on top of processor terms. Check What the Vendor Will Actually Process Before Reviewing the Clauses Start with the processing annex and the business’s intended use, not the vendor’s liability cap. The most polished DPA isn’t very useful if its description of the service is wrong. Compare the agreement and its schedules with the order form, statement of work, vendor questionnaire, and what the business sponsor has actually asked the vendor to do. Information to verify Check against Why it matters Purpose, services, and duration Processing annex, order form, SOW It defines scope and permitted use Personal data and affected individuals Data inventory, intake questionnaire It surfaces sensitivity and exposure Contracting parties and roles DPA definitions, entity list It clarifies who gives instructions Storage, support, and access locations Hosting map, security documentation It identifies transfer and access risks Subprocessors and onward processing Current subprocessor list, service diagram It enables authorization and oversight For example, a DPA that only refers to business contact details needs another look if the deployment will give the vendor access to customer records or employee files. Update the description and risk assessment before debating narrower drafting points because the rest of the review depends on getting these facts right. Over the past fifteen years, I have had the good fortune to work alongside — and across the table from — some of the most capable and dedicated lawyers in government. What has stayed with me is the sense of purpose they bring to their work: a deep commitment to serving others and taking on matters whose impact extends far beyond themselves. These roles demand deep subject-matter expertise, sound judgment, and an understanding of the institutions those lawyers serve. Government lawyers perform some of the most consequential work in our profession. They advise the institutions responsible for delivering public services, help determine how public resources are spent, and handle complex litigation and investigations on behalf of the public. Their decisions can affect individuals, businesses, and communities far beyond the immediate matter in front of them. This is why serving government lawyers matters to us at Harvey. The Opportunity for Legal AI in Government We’re working to transform the practice of law and improve the lives of lawyers everywhere. We cannot do that if we don’t support public sector lawyers . Our public sector lawyers deserve access to the best tools our profession has to offer, designed and deployed in safe and secure ways that meet the demands of their work. For Harvey, improving legal practice includes helping public institutions make better use of the expertise of the lawyers who work within them. Those lawyers often carry substantial workloads, with competing demands on their time and limited flexibility to add capacity. Alongside the work that requires their judgment, they spend hours reviewing records, assembling facts, locating prior analysis, and preparing initial drafts. When experienced colleagues retire or move to new roles, deciphering the institutional knowledge behind an earlier decision can become a project of its own. These tasks are essential to legal practice, but they also create opportunities for better tools to make a meaningful difference. Helping a lawyer work through a large record or locate relevant institutional knowledge can give them more time for substantive analysis, to test an argument, advise a colleague, or prepare for a consequential decision that affects the public. blogs.content: Insights How Mid-Sized Firms are Building an AI Advantage Four mid-sized law firm leaders share how they’re using AI to extend partner expertise, build firmwide adoption, compete with leaner teams, and work with clients in new ways. by Harvey Team • Nov 18, 2026 A large firm’s traditional edge was its bench: more lawyers to staff a matter and work through the details. AI is changing how much that staffing advantage matters, giving mid-sized firms new ways to put their existing expertise to work. At Harvey FORUM Chicago, Daniel Berkowitz, Partner at Cruser Mitchell; Laura Jakubowski, Director of Knowledge Management and Innovation at Goldberg Kohn; Patrick Croke, Founding Partner and CEO at Croke Fairchild Duarte & Beres; and Sonia Menon, Chief Operating Officer at Neal, Gerber & Eisenberg, discussed what AI is changing about how mid-sized firms compete. Their experiences point to a clear opportunity for mid-sized firms: use AI to apply their expertise across more of the work clients bring them. Bring Partner Judgment Into More of the Work At Croke Fairchild Duarte & Beres, the staffing model reflects a deliberate choice. The firm is comfortable with a partner-heavy structure, where a partner with decades of experience may work directly on a merger or employment agreement. Patrick Croke sees AI as a way to make that model more efficient while helping the firm train younger lawyers faster. Watch Video That approach brings client work and lawyer development together. A partner’s experience informs the agreement, while younger lawyers can learn how that judgment is applied. In this model, the work itself gives senior lawyers a way to help the next generation build the skills they’ll need to take on more responsibility. Make AI an Ongoing Leadership Conversation As AI’s capabilities advance, firms need to keep discussing where it fits into their work and how they want to use it. At Neal, Gerber & Eisenberg, AI is a standing agenda item at executive committee meetings every three weeks and partner meetings every two months. Sonia Menon said the discussions cover client questions, new use cases, cost, risk, and repeatability. Watch Video The conversation continues in client relationships, where senior partners are already discussing AI and helping drive its adoption. As Menon described it, the partners leading those client conversations are also helping shape how the technology is introduced across the firm. Give Adoption a Cross-Firm Structure When Laura Jakubowski began organizing Goldberg Kohn’s AI committee, she wanted people who were interested in the work and represented the firm’s different perspectives. That meant looking beyond lawyers to include the people who support and move legal work forward across the firm. Watch Video The committee includes at least one person from each practice group, along with partners, associates, operations staff, legal secretaries, and paralegals. Its breadth gives Jakubowski a way to hear how AI questions and opportunities look across different roles. And the structure is intentionally modest: members make a small time commitment, with no additional headcount or budget. For firms still figuring out who should be involved, Jakubowski found that a focused committee was a useful place to start. Compete on Rates With a Leaner Team For much of legal practice, larger firms had an advantage because they could put more people on a matter. Daniel Berkowitz sees that gap narrowing as firms of different sizes use the same AI tools. Watch Video Berkowitz says clients are starting to question how many lawyers a matter requires. He points to a one-partner, one-associate team as a model that can extend to more sophisticated work. blogs.description: Harvey’s Head of Legal Innovation, Law Firms, AMER, Megan McMillin on what to settle before a firm approves its 2027 technology budget, from renewal deadlines to matter economics.
blogs.content: Insights Planning Your Law Firm’s 2027 Technology Budget by Megan McMillin • Nov 16, 2026 Preparing a law firm’s technology budget means working through requests that serve different purposes. Some spending keeps the firm’s existing systems reliable. Other investments help a practice take on new work or develop a service for clients. The firm also needs to decide how much it can spend testing ideas whose value it has yet to establish. The Three Horizons framework offers a useful comparison. It describes how organizations can support their core business while developing emerging opportunities and exploring future possibilities. Applied to technology budgeting, it helps explain why a system replacement and an experiment need different justifications. Both need a clear purpose, but the firm cannot expect the same level of certainty from each. 1. Connect spending to the firm’s priorities The firm’s plans give context to individual technology requests. A corporate practice expecting more transactions may need to reduce the time lawyers spend preparing first drafts. A new practice may need specialist research sources. Understanding the work behind a request makes it easier to assess its importance and explain why it deserves funding. Those requests sit alongside existing contractual commitments and the cost of keeping core systems operating securely and reliably. Finance, technology, and practice leaders need a shared view of those obligations when they discuss what the firm can take on next. Dependencies also affect the decision. A new knowledge tool may require the firm to organize its documents and correct access permissions before lawyers can use it effectively. The proposal needs to account for that work. Otherwise, the firm risks approving a purchase without funding the conditions that would make it useful. For each significant request, the budget discussion should establish what the firm expects to improve and what would happen if it waited another year. That gives leaders a practical basis for comparing proposals that address different needs. 2. Reassess existing tools before renewing them A complete view of technology spending includes central IT purchases, tools that practice groups buy directly, and subscriptions that individuals expense. Looking across those purchases can reveal overlapping costs or capabilities the firm already owns. Usage data helps, but it needs context. A product with few users may serve a small practice doing important specialist work. The lawyers who rely on it can explain what it contributes and what they would need instead. Low adoption can also reflect a training problem rather than a lack of demand for the tool. Contract timing matters when the firm identifies something it could replace. If an existing contract runs through September, a replacement that starts in January will create a period when the firm pays for both. The budget needs to reflect that overlap and any migration costs. Renewal notice deadlines therefore deserve attention before the firm counts on savings. The relevant number is the amount the firm can actually stop spending during the budget year, after accounting for the cost of the transition. 3. Budget for the work required to implement the technology The vendor’s price will not cover everything the firm needs to contribute. A project may require document migration, integration with other systems, and work on permissions. The budget should distinguish the services the vendor provides from the work the firm will handle itself. Internal time deserves particular attention. An AI rollout may depend on the same IT and knowledge teams that are already working on a document management upgrade. Each project can look manageable on its own. blogs.content: 返回博客 如何用 AutoClaw 核对采购发票与订单 教程 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月27日 月底核对供应商发票，难点不在一张张看金额：发票要和采购订单、入库单三方对上，部分到货的开票数量常常多于入库数量，调价前后的单价混在一起，税率、抬头开错的要退回重开，同一张发票还可能被重复提交。本文以一家公司 11 月的 86 张采购发票为例，讲怎么用 AutoClaw 核对采购发票与订单——核对规则一次写清、按规则跑出第一版差异清单、收到回复后只更新有差异的发票、入账前逐项核对。 如何用 AutoClaw 核对采购发票与订单 每到月底，做应付的财务同事都要过一遍当月收到的供应商发票：哪些可以入账，哪些要退回，哪些还得等采购补手续。发票本身只有“发票号、供应商、金额”几列，可是要入账，就得回头翻采购订单和仓库的入库单，看数量、单价、税率是否都对得上。 手工核对最容易出错的地方有三个：一张订单分几次到货、几次开票，开票数量和入库数量要跨表累计才能比；供应商中途调过价，有的发票按新价开、订单还是旧价，看金额差几百元，不知道该退还是该补审批；发票邮件和纸质件各收一份，同一张发票被提交两次，不仔细比对发票号就会重复入账。 这次我们用 AutoClaw，以「11 月采购发票核对」为例，四步完成写清核对规则、跑出第一版差异清单、收到回复后只更新差异发票和入账前核对。 本案例中的供应商、订单、发票和金额均为任务设定的示例数据。 第一步：把数据和核对规则写清 在 AutoClaw 新建一个任务，本次使用 GLM-5.3-Flash，上传三份文件：11 月发票清单（从发票平台导出）、采购订单明细和仓库入库单明细。发票核对出问题，多半是因为“差多少算对得上”只在财务同事心里有数，所以提示词先交代数据范围，再把每一条口径写成能检查的句子，最后说明要交付什么、怎么核对。 本次案例使用的完整提示词： 帮我核对 11 月的采购发票，输出 Excel。 1. **数据**：附件「11月发票清单.xlsx」是本月收到的全部发票，共 86 张，来自 23 家供应商；「采购订单明细.xlsx」是相关的 74 张订单；「入库单明细.xlsx」是 91 张入库单。 2. **匹配**：按发票备注或明细里的订单号对应采购订单，再按订单号和物料编码对应入库单。一张订单分几次到货、几次开票的，按累计数比较。 3. **数量**：以入库单为准，累计开票数量不能超过累计入库数量。 4. **单价和税率**：以订单为准；含税金额差在 ±1 元以内算尾差，视为一致。 5. **抬头和重复**：发票抬头、税号必须与本公司一致；同一发票号只能入账一次。 6. **交付**：三张表——核对明细表（每张发票的匹配结果）、差异清单（写明原因和依据的单号）、可入账汇总。 7. **完成后核对**：发票张数、含税合计和发票清单一致；每张差异发票都有原因和依据。 红线：找不到订单的发票不要按供应商和金额猜着配，列进差异清单。 提示词里最重要的是第 2、3、4 条。“按累计数比较”“数量以入库为准”“±1 元以内算尾差”这类口径写成能检查的句子，AutoClaw 核对每一张发票时都会对照，最后也能逐张说明依据；如果只写一句“帮我看看这些发票有没有问题”，它只能按单张金额去比订单，分批到货的发票会被大量误报，真正多开的数量反而淹没在里面。 红线一条管的是“订单里找不到”的情况。按供应商和金额去凑一张最像的订单，看起来省事，可一旦配错，后面付款、对账都会跟着错；列进差异清单，问一句采购，往往就清楚了。 第二步：按规则跑出第一版差异清单 本次任务中，AutoClaw 先读完三份文件，把 86 张发票逐张对到订单和入库单上。71 张三单一致，可以直接入账，含税合计 1,962,310.00 元；其余 15 张有差异，含税合计 406,230.00 元，按原因分成六类： 数量不符 6 张：供应商按订单全量开票，仓库只入库了一部分。 单价不符 3 张：发票按 11 月调价后的单价开，订单还是调价前的价格。 税率不符 2 张：技术服务费订单约定 6%，发票开成了 13%。 找不到订单 2 张：发票上的订单号在订单明细里查不到。 重复发票 1 张：同一发票号在清单里出现了两次。 抬头错误 1 张：税号少了一位。 差异清单出来了，还要再看一眼“找不到订单”这一类。 按红线，这 2 张没有被硬配到某张订单上，而是附上了发票号、供应商和金额单独列出。我们拿去问采购，1 张是采购下单时漏建了系统订单，另 1 张其实是供应商开给集团另一家子公司的，被误寄到了这边。 这正是先看清单、再入账的意义：如果当时按金额凑了一张订单，开给子公司的那张发票就会进入本公司的账，等对方来要时，再冲销就麻烦多了。 第三步：收到回复后，只更新有差异的发票 差异清单发给采购和供应商后，几天内陆续收到回复：数量不符的 6 张中，4 张的剩余货物已经补货入库，另 2 张供应商同意红冲后按实际入库数量重开；单价不符的 3 张中，2 张由采购补走了调价审批，另 1 张供应商同意按订单价重开；税率不符的 2 张按 6% 重开；漏建订单的 1 张采购已补建；抬头错误的 1 张退回重开。 在原任务里补一句：“附件是采购和供应商的回复，以及补货的入库单和补建的订单。只更新这 15 张差异发票的状态，已经核对一致的 71 张不要动，改了哪些列出来，V1 另存。” AutoClaw 只更新了这 15 张：补货入库的 4 张、补了调价审批的 2 张和补建订单的 1 张重新核对后一致，新增可入账 7 张，可入账从 71 张变为 78 张，含税合计 2,230,760.00 元；待供应商重开 6 张，112,600.00 元；开给子公司的 1 张退回，18,960.00 元；重复的 1 张拦截，6,220.00 元，不进入入账汇总。生成了 V2。 这里值得留意的是“已经核对一致的不要动”这几个字。如果只说“按最新资料重新核对一遍”，AutoClaw 会从头再跑一次，结果大概率一样，但对照起来费劲，也说不清这一轮到底解决了哪几张。把范围限定在差异发票上，变动清单一眼就能看完。 第四步：入账前核对四处 V2 交付时，AutoClaw 按提示词里的核对要求逐项报告了结果。提交入账之前，我们只需要看四处： 张数对得上：可入账 78 张、待重开 6 张、退回 1 张、拦截 1 张，合计 86 张，和发票清单一致。 金额对得上：四类含税合计 2,368,540.00 元，和发票清单的合计一致；V1 的 1,962,310.00 元加上新增可入账的 268,450.00 元，正好是 2,230,760.00 元。 每张有依据：15 张差异发票都写明了原因，附上订单号、入库单号和供应商或采购的回复。 重复不入账：同号的 1 张发票已拦截，可入账汇总里同一发票号只出现一次。 四项核对十来分钟就能过完。交给主管审批的入账汇总，每张发票为什么能入、为什么退回都有依据；下个月供应商来问“那张发票怎么还没付款”，翻差异清单就能回答。 用 AutoClaw 核对采购发票与订单 AutoClaw 帮助做应付的财务同事把发票、订单、入库单的比对放进同一个任务：核对口径一次写清，三方数据自动对到同一张表，收到回复时只更新有差异的发票，每一版都附带依据和核对结果。财务同事不用再在三张表之间来回筛选，可以把精力放在跟进供应商重开、和采购理清调价流程上。 下个月核对时，可以沿用这次的提示词，只替换三份附件，匹配、数量和尾差的口径都不用重写。 下载 AutoClaw，体验发票核对 → 常见问题 AutoClaw 核对出“一致”的发票就可以直接入账吗？ 写进提示词的口径会逐条执行，每一张发票都能说明对上了哪张订单和入库单。没写进去的规则它不会自己知道，比如某类费用必须附合同，就要在提示词里写清。入账前建议按第四步抽查几张。 发票上没写订单号，还能匹配吗？ 可以在提示词里补一条备用规则，比如“没有订单号的，按供应商、物料名称和数量匹配，匹配结果标为待确认”。这样匹配出来的发票会单独标出，由财务确认后再入账，不会和按订单号对上的混在一起。 发票清单是从发票平台导出的，格式比较乱，能处理吗？ 可以直接上传导出的 Excel 或 CSV。AutoClaw 会先识别发票号、供应商、金额、税率和备注；遇到同一供应商名称写法不统一、金额带千分位或文字这类情况，会先统一写法再核对，处理方式写在明细表的备注里。 尾差容差应该设多少？ 按公司的财务制度来。常见做法是含税金额差在 1 元以内视为尾差，也有公司按比例设，比如差额不超过 0.1%。写进提示词后，AutoClaw 会在明细表里单独标出“按尾差处理”的发票，方便复核。 核对结果能直接发给供应商吗？ 建议先由财务和采购确认差异清单再发。确认后可以让 AutoClaw 按供应商拆成一份份退票说明，只保留该供应商的发票号、差异原因和需要重开的内容，订单价格和其他供应商的信息不会出现在里面。 下载 AutoClaw，体验发票核对 →

blogs.content: 返回博客 如何用 AutoClaw 起草法律文书？从案件材料到文书初稿 教程 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月27日 本文以一起未签书面劳动合同的二倍工资争议为例，演示用 AutoClaw 法律助手的智能文书起草，从案件材料生成劳动仲裁申请书、金额计算表、证据目录和待补材料清单，再经第二轮复核完善，并附两段可复用的提示词。 准备一份劳动仲裁申请书，往往不只是把事情经过写下来。 入职通知、劳动合同、工资记录、考勤信息和工作沟通记录，可能分散在不同材料中。如何从这些信息中梳理案件事实、明确仲裁请求、核算相关金额，并最终形成一份结构完整的申请书？ 借助 AI 法律助手，这些工作能否在一个连续的工作流中完成？ 这次，我们以一起未及时订立书面劳动合同的劳动争议为例，看看 AutoClaw 如何从案件材料出发，协助完成劳动仲裁申请书及相关附件的起草，并通过后续复核进一步完善文书。 一、从法律助手到智能文书起草 在 AutoClaw 中，法律文书起草可以从专门的法律功能入口开始。 进入 AutoClaw 后，选择 「法律助手」 ，并根据任务需要选择对应的法律模型。本次演示使用的是 GLM-5.3-FlashX-Legal ，面向法律场景开展后续任务。 在法律助手的功能入口中，还可以进一步选择 「智能文书起草」 。进入后，根据实际任务选择文书类型，例如： 合同起草 一审文书 二审文书 再审文书 执行文书 客户向文书 保全文书 仲裁文书 本次选择的是「仲裁文书」下的 「劳动仲裁申请书」 。 通过这一入口，使用者可以直接进入对应的文书起草任务，再结合具体案件上传材料、补充要求，而不必完全从空白对话开始组织任务。 【配图1｜AutoClaw 法律助手、GLM-5.3-FlashX-Legal 模型及智能文书起草入口】 二、从案件材料到文书成果：三个值得关注的细节 本次演示准备了两组模拟材料： 案件说明与委托要求：介绍当事人情况、入职经过、工资标准、签约过程及本次委托范围。 模拟证据材料：包含入职通知、签约通信记录、工资发放摘录、考勤记录及劳动合同相关信息，统一编号为 E01—E05。 模拟案件中，劳动者于2026年6月1日实际入职，正常工作时间固定月工资为8,700元。入职后，劳动者曾两次通过工作通信催促签订书面劳动合同，但用人单位以内部合同模板审批为由推迟，直至2026年8月18日才首次完成书面合同签署。 劳动者希望就未及时订立书面劳动合同期间的二倍工资差额申请劳动仲裁，并明确本次只处理这一项请求，不涉及社保、解除劳动合同、经济补偿或加班费。 我们将上述材料上传至 AutoClaw，要求其站在劳动者立场，结合中国大陆法律及北京地区相关裁审口径，起草劳动仲裁申请书，并整理配套附件。 最终形成的文书成果主要体现在以下三个方面。 从案件经过到明确的仲裁请求 劳动仲裁申请书首先需要回答：当事人是谁、发生了什么争议、希望仲裁机构裁决什么。 本次案件的信息分散在入职通知、工作通信、工资记录和劳动合同等材料中。 AutoClaw 将这些信息整理为申请书的主要组成部分： 当事人信息：整理申请人与被申请人的基本信息，对材料未提供的身份信息和主体信息标记待补。 仲裁请求：根据委托范围，明确本次仅主张未订立书面劳动合同的二倍工资差额。 事实与理由：按照劳动关系建立、工资支付、催促签约、实际签署劳动合同等事项组织事实。 法律依据：结合劳动合同法及相关劳动争议裁审规则，说明请求所依据的规范。 最终，申请书将仲裁请求明确为： 请求裁决被申请人向申请人支付2026年7月2日至2026年8月17日期间未订立书面劳动合同的二倍工资差额人民币13,200元。 同时，申请书保留了身份证号码、住所、企业统一社会信用代码等尚未提供的信息，没有自行补造。 从分散的案件信息到结构化的申请书，AutoClaw 帮助使用者将事实材料组织为可以继续核对和修改的文书初稿。 【配图2｜劳动仲裁申请书首页及仲裁请求】 请求金额如何与计算过程对应？ 法律文书中的金额不仅要有最终结果，还需要能够说明计算依据。 本次演示中，AutoClaw 在申请书之外，单独整理了请求金额计算表，将计算期间、工资基数、实际工作日及分段金额列示出来。 本次复核后的计算结果如下： 计算期间 实际工作日 金额 2026年7月2日至7月31日 22天 8,800元 2026年8月1日至8月17日 11天 4,400元 合计 33天 13,200元 计算表还进一步说明： 工资基数为正常工作时间固定税前月工资8,700元； 日工资按照月计薪天数21.75天折算； 不满一个月的期间按照适用规则及实际工作日计算； 7月1日为满一个月的最后一日，8月18日为书面劳动合同订立日，均不计入本次计算期间。 在后续复核中，AutoClaw 重新核对了相关日期、日历和考勤材料，并独立计算各期间金额。 最终，申请书中的13,200元与附件一计算表保持一致，计算过程也能够逐项查看。 这让请求金额不再只是申请书中的一个数字，而是有相应的计算依据和核对过程。 【配图3｜请求金额计算表及分段计算结果】 证据目录如何与案件事实对应？ 除了申请书和金额计算表，本次演示还生成了证据目录及待补材料清单。 AutoClaw 将原始模拟材料沿用的 E01—E05 编号整理到证据目录中，并说明每项材料能够证明什么。 编号 证据名称 对应事实 E01 入职通知及登记信息 实际入职时间、岗位及工作安排 E02 签约通信记录 两次催签经过及公司延迟签约的情况 E03 工资发放摘录 固定工资标准及支付情况 E04 考勤记录 工作时间及实际工作日 E05 劳动合同相关字段及签署记录 合同实际签署日期及合同期限 此外，AutoClaw 还整理了附件三《待补材料清单》，将身份证明、企业主体信息、原始通信记录、银行流水、考勤原始记录及劳动合同原件等事项列出。 其中，7月逐日考勤记录在现有模拟材料中只有文字说明，因此被保留为待补事项，而没有被描述成已经取得的原始证据。 证据目录与待补清单的配合，使申请书中的事实能够进一步对应到具体材料，也方便使用者继续准备和整理仲裁所需文件。 【配图4｜附件二证据目录与附件三待补材料清单】 三、从初稿生成到二次复核：让文书进一步完善 对于法律文书起草而言，生成初稿只是一个阶段。 本次演示中，我们没有直接将首轮生成的 Word 作为最终成果，而是进一步要求 AutoClaw 重新读取最初上传的案件说明与证据材料，对申请书及附件开展第二轮复核。 这一轮主要围绕四个方面展开： 第一，核对案件事实与证据。 重新检查入职日期、工资标准、催签记录、劳动合同签署日期及在职情况，确认相关事实能够在 E01—E05 中找到对应依据。 第二，复核法律依据与适用规则。 结合劳动合同法、劳动合同法实施条例、最高人民法院劳动争议司法解释及北京地区相关裁审口径，检查规范的现行效力、具体条文及其适用条件。 第三，独立核算请求金额。 重新核对计算期间、工资基数、实际工作日和日工资折算方式，确保申请书与金额计算表中的数据一致。 第四，检查文书及附件之间的对应关系。 检查仲裁请求、事实理由、计算表、证据目录和待补材料清单之间的日期、金额及证据编号，确保各项内容能够相互对应。 完成复核后，AutoClaw 输出了复核清单，逐项列明核验结果、依据和处理方式，并在此基础上生成修订版 Word。 本次复核后的文书保留了原有仲裁请求及13,200元金额，并对事实表述、法律依据、期间计算说明和附件表述进行了完善。 通过“初稿生成—二次复核—修订交付”的多轮操作，使用者可以在初稿基础上继续检查和完善内容，而不是将首次生成的结果直接作为最终版本。 【配图5｜第二轮复核提示词】 【配图6｜第二轮复核清单】 四、自己试试：两段可复用的法律文书起草提示词 本次演示采用了两轮交互。第一轮负责根据案件材料生成初稿，第二轮则围绕原始材料、法律依据及文书一致性开展复核。 如果你也想尝试，可以分别使用下面两段提示词。 Prompt 01｜劳动仲裁申请书起草 请根据我上传的案件说明及相关证据材料，站在【劳动者/用人单位】的立场，协助准备一套劳动仲裁文书。 本次争议的主要情况是：【简要说明争议类型、劳动关系建立情况及争议经过】。 我的具体请求范围是：【列明希望提出的仲裁请求，并明确不涉及的事项】。 请结合案件材料及现行有效的中国大陆法律法规，依次完成： 劳动仲裁申请书：整理当事人信息、仲裁请求、事实与理由及相关法律依据。 请求金额计算表：列明计算期间、工资基数、计算方法、分项金额及合计，并说明对应依据。 证据目录：逐项列出证据名称、证明目的及对应的案件事实。 待补材料清单：列明现有材料缺失或需要进一步核实的信息。 请严格遵循以下要求： 区分案件材料已经明确的事实、当事人的陈述及尚待核实的事项。 不自行补充身份证号码、企业信息、签署日期、工资金额等未知事实。 仲裁请求应严格遵循我的委托范围，不擅自增加其他请求。 法律依据应注明规范名称、具体条文及可核验来源。 blogs.content: 返回博客 如何用 AutoClaw 排年会座位表 教程 作者：AutoClaw Team 2026年11月26日 年会排座位，难点不在把人填进桌子：主桌、节目组和客户桌位置固定，同部门要尽量坐在一起，拼桌的小部门不能太散，每桌要有人带桌，素食、清真的份数还要按桌报给酒店，报名截止后又总有人加进来、有人取消。本文以一场 312 人的公司年会为例，讲怎么用 AutoClaw 排年会座位表——排座规则一次写清、按规则排出第一版、报名变动后只调整受影响的桌、发出前逐项核对。 如何用 AutoClaw 排年会座位表 每到 12 月，做行政或活动的同事都会接到同一件事：年会报名收齐了，要排出座位表，一份给酒店摆桌、备餐，一份发给大家找座位。表本身只有“桌号、姓名、部门”几列，可大家拿到后，总会顺着自己的位置问：“我们组怎么被拆到两桌去了？”“我报了素食，酒店那边知道吗？” 手工排座最容易出错的地方有三个：主桌、节目组桌和客户桌位置固定，剩下的人按部门排，大部门要拆成整桌、小部门要拼桌，拼来拼去很容易漏人或重复；报名表里有人重复提交、有人饮食偏好没填，直接照着排就会多出空位或备错餐；报名截止后还会陆续有人加进来、有人取消，每改一次都从头排，已经通知过的座位全被打乱。 这次我们用 AutoClaw，以「2026 年度公司年会座位安排」为例，四步完成写清排座规则、按规则排出第一版、报名变动后只调整受影响的桌和发出前核对。 本案例中的人员、部门、桌数和酒店场地均为任务设定的示例数据。 第一步：把数据和排座规则写清 在 AutoClaw 新建一个任务，本次使用 GLM-5.3-Flash，上传三份文件：年会报名表、员工花名册（含部门和职级），以及酒店给的宴会厅平面图。座位排不好，多半是因为规则只在行政同事脑子里，所以提示词先交代数据范围，再把每一条规则写成能检查的句子，最后说明要交付什么、怎么核对。 本次案例使用的完整提示词： 帮我排 2026 年度公司年会的座位表，输出 Excel，另出一张平面示意图。 1. **数据**：附件「年会报名表.xlsx」是全部报名记录；「花名册.xlsx」有每个人的部门和职级；「宴会厅平面图.pdf」是酒店场地，共 27 桌，每桌 12 人，1 号桌在舞台正前方，入口在 25～27 号桌一侧。 2. **固定桌**：1 号桌是主桌，坐公司高管 8 人和特邀客户 4 人；2、3 号桌给节目组 24 人，靠近后台方便上场；4 号桌坐另外 4 位特邀客户和对接的销售。 3. **按部门排**：其余人同部门尽量坐在一起；一个部门超过 12 人的拆成整桌，不足一桌的小部门拼桌，每桌最多拼 3 个部门。 4. **带桌**：除 1～3 号桌外，每桌至少有 1 位经理及以上职级的同事负责带桌。 5. **特殊需求**：行动不便的同事安排在靠近入口的桌；素食、清真按桌统计份数。 6. **交付**：三张表——座位明细表（桌号、姓名、部门、餐食）、按桌汇总的餐食份数（给酒店）、待确认清单。 7. **完成后核对**：报名人数和入座人数对得上；每桌不超过 12 人；每桌都有带桌人。 红线：报名表里部门或饮食偏好没填的不要猜，列进待确认清单。 提示词里最重要的是第 2、3、4 条。“1 号桌坐谁”“每桌最多拼 3 个部门”“每桌至少 1 位带桌人”这类规则写成能检查的句子，AutoClaw 排每一桌时都会对照，最后也能逐桌说明依据；如果只写一句“帮我把报名的人排一下座位”，它只能按报名顺序往桌子里填，同部门被拆散、带桌人扎堆坐在一起都很常见，大家一看就有意见。 红线一条管的是“报名表没写”的情况。比如有人饮食偏好一栏是空的，这时最稳妥的是问本人，表里只需要列出来，而不是默认给他配普通餐，到了现场才发现吃不了。 第二步：按规则排出第一版座位 本次任务中，AutoClaw 先读完三份文件，把报名表和花名册逐人对上：报名表共 315 行，有 3 人用同一工号提交了两次，去重后实际报名 312 人。1～4 号桌按规则先排好固定的 48 人，其余 264 人按部门排进 5～27 号桌：研发、销售、市场等大部门拆成整桌，财务、法务、行政等小部门拼桌。 V1 排下来，27 桌里 24 桌坐满 12 人，25 号桌 10 人、26 号桌 9 人、27 号桌 5 人，空出 12 个座位。2 位行动不便的同事安排在靠近入口的 25 号桌。餐食方面，素食 11 份、清真 4 份，已按桌汇总。 座位排出来了，还要再看一眼待确认清单。 按红线，报名表里有 2 人的饮食偏好没填，被单独列出，V1 暂按普通餐统计，没有替他们做决定。我们问过本人，1 人吃素、1 人普通餐，素食份数从 11 份变为 12 份。 这正是先看清单、再发结论的意义：酒店的备餐单一旦确认，临时加素食往往来不及；在发出前把这 2 个人问清，比到了现场再协调省事得多。 第三步：报名变动后，只调整受影响的桌 V1 发给各部门确认的第二天，行政收到了报名变动：销售部新入职的 3 人要参加，另有 2 位外部嘉宾确认出席，其中 1 位吃素；研发部 2 人、市场部 1 人因出差取消。在原任务里补一句：“附件是报名变动清单，新增 5 人、取消 3 人。只调整受影响的桌，已经确认过的座位尽量不动，改了哪几桌列出来，V1 另存。” AutoClaw 只动了 4 桌：取消的 3 人从 9 号桌（研发部）和 15 号桌（市场部）移出，两桌分别变为 10 人和 11 人；新入职的 3 人排进 27 号桌，从 5 人变为 8 人；2 位外部嘉宾排进 26 号桌，从 9 人变为 11 人。入座总人数从 312 人变为 314 人，其余 23 桌一个座位都没动，生成了 V2。 这里值得留意的是“尽量不动”这几个字。如果只说“按最新名单重新排”，AutoClaw 会从头排一遍，结果可能更整齐，但已经通知到各部门的桌号会大面积变化，大家又要重新找座位。把“只调整受影响的桌”写进要求，改动就被控制在 4 桌之内，变动清单也一眼能看完。 V1 另存在原文件夹里，改动的 4 桌单独列了一张对照表。有人问“我的桌号是不是变了”，直接翻这张表就能回答。 第四步：发出前核对四处 V2 交付时，AutoClaw 按提示词里的核对要求逐项报告了结果。发给酒店和全员之前，我们只需要看四处： 人数对得上：报名去重后 312 人，加上新增 5 人、减去取消 3 人，共 314 人，和座位明细表的入座人数一致，没有漏排或重复。 每桌不超员：27 桌都不超过 12 人，空出的 10 个座位在 9、15、25、26、27 号桌，可以给现场临时来的同事。 带桌有人：4～27 号桌每桌都有 1 位经理及以上职级的同事带桌，拼桌的桌每桌不超过 3 个部门。 餐食报得准：素食 13 份、清真 4 份、普通餐 297 份，按桌写清份数，2 位饮食偏好待确认的同事已经问过本人。 四项核对十来分钟就能过完。发出去的座位表，每个人的位置都能说清依据；大家追问为什么坐这一桌、素食报上去没有，都能在表里直接找到答案，不用再回头翻报名表。 用 AutoClaw 排年会座位表 AutoClaw 帮助做行政和活动的同事把排座、统计和核对放进同一个任务：排座规则一次写清，报名表和花名册自动对到同一张表，报名有变动时只调整受影响的桌，每一版都附带依据和核对结果。行政同事不用再在报名表和平面图之间来回比对，可以把精力放在节目流程、现场布置和嘉宾接待上。 明年排座时，可以沿用这次的提示词，只替换报名表和平面图附件，固定桌、按部门排和带桌的规则都不用重写。 下载 AutoClaw，体验年会座位安排 会按新的容量重排，并把桌号变化列出来。场地定下来之前，建议先不要把桌号发给全员。 报名表是问卷导出的，格式比较乱，能处理吗？ 可以直接上传问卷导出的 Excel 或 CSV。AutoClaw 会先识别姓名、工号、部门和饮食偏好；遇到同一人重复提交、部门写法不统一这类情况，会先去重和统一写法再排座，处理方式写在明细表的备注里。 现场有人临时来了怎么办？ 座位表里空出的座位会单独列出，现场可以直接安排。年会前一天再让 AutoClaw 按最新名单出一版“空位清单”，标出每个空位在哪一桌、旁边是哪个部门，现场签到的同事拿着就能用。 座位表能直接发给全员吗？ 建议先把待确认清单里的问题处理完再发。确认后可以让 AutoClaw 另出一份按姓名排序的查座表，只保留姓名、部门和桌号，餐食和职级信息只留在给酒店和行政的版本里。 下载
